prediction.likelyOutcome: Covenant has the better of the extrinsic evidence on whether Section 3(c) was a condition precedent, and has already survived Empower's summary attempt to resolve that question as a matter of law, but the trial court's own ambiguity finding means this is a genuine jury question rather than a likely runaway win. Most probable outcome is a jury finding for Covenant on the condition-precedent theory (return of the $96,291.09 deposit, no commencement, and defeat of Empower's breach claim), though a verdict for Empower remains a real possibility given the hard outside dates built into Exhibit G's commencement mechanics; Empower's fraud counterclaim is unlikely to survive regardless of the condition-precedent ruling.

issues.label: Section 3(c) as Condition Precedent vs. Covenant

figures.label: Deposit paid by Covenant to Empower
figures.quote: Covenant paid Empower $96,291.09 as a deposit.

issues.label: Procedural Posture — Denial of Empower's Rule 248 Motion

outcome.description: After a four-day jury trial the jury found Section 3(c) was a condition precedent that Empower failed to satisfy; the trial court rendered judgment declaring the lease abrogated and ordered Empower to pay Covenant $96,291.09 in damages (the deposit), $611,491.45 in attorney's fees, and $135,000 in conditional appellate fees. The court of appeals held Section 3(c) is a covenant, not a condition precedent, reversed the entire judgment, rendered take-nothing on the condition-precedent declarations, and remanded the remaining declarations, the damages and fee awards, and Empower's breach-of-contract counterclaim.
outcome.finalNote: Reversed and remanded; no final figure yet.
